title: Week 7 Mastery Quiz — Persia and the Greek World

questions.prompt: What was a satrapy in the Achaemenid Persian Empire?
choices: A Greek citizen assembly
An administrative province within the empire
A military alliance among poleis
A category of Spartan laborer
questions.explanation: A satrapy was an administrative province within the Persian imperial system.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the Greek polis?
choices: A city-state and its civic community, with political institutions that varied among poleis
A province governed by a Persian satrap
A unified Greek national government
A Persian road station
questions.explanation: A polis was a Greek city-state and civic community; Greek poleis had varied institutions.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Athenian democracy is most accurate for the classical period?
choices: All adult residents participated equally.
Women and enslaved people voted but foreigners did not.
Direct political participation expanded for a restricted body of male citizens while many residents remained excluded.
Athens used representative elections identical to modern democracies.
questions.explanation: Athenian democracy enabled substantial direct participation for male citizens while excluding women, enslaved people, and resident foreigners from citizenship.

questions.prompt: Why is describing the Persian Empire simply as “tolerant” historically incomplete?
choices: Persian rulers prohibited all local customs.
The empire had no central government.
Accommodation occurred only in Greek cities.
Local institutions and practices could continue, but within an unequal imperial system sustained by taxation, loyalty demands, and coercive power.
questions.explanation: Accommodation and local continuity coexisted with imperial hierarchy and coercive authority.

questions.prompt: Which evidence would best help a historian test a Greek author’s claim about Persian imperial rule?
choices: Persian inscriptions, administrative records, archaeology, and other independent evidence
A second quotation from the same sentence
A modern fictional retelling only
The assumption that primary sources are always accurate
questions.explanation: Corroboration across independent Persian and material evidence helps test narrative claims.

choices: Rejecting every source with a point of view
Interpreting actions and claims within their historical conditions while evaluating source position and evidence
Assuming ancient people shared modern political definitions
Choosing the source whose values are closest to ours
questions.explanation: Historical perspective contextualizes actors and sources without suspending evidence-based evaluation.

questions.prompt: Why is Sparta important to a comparison of the Greek political world?
choices: It proves every polis was democratic.
It was governed as a Persian satrapy.
Its distinctive institutions and dependence on an exploited helot population show that Greek political organization varied sharply among poleis.
It included every resident as an equal citizen.
questions.explanation: Sparta demonstrates major institutional and status differences within the Greek world.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest criticism of a simple “Greek freedom versus Persian tyranny” interpretation?
choices: There were no meaningful institutional differences between Athens and Persia.
Persia was actually a direct democracy.
Greek sources contain no usable evidence.
The frame can obscure restricted citizenship, slavery, differences among Greek poleis, Greek coercion, and Persian forms of local accommodation.
questions.explanation: The binary can preserve one contrast while concealing other structures of participation, hierarchy, coercion, and negotiation.

questions.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes citizenship from residence?
choices: Citizenship defines recognized political membership with particular rights and duties; residence alone does not necessarily confer that status.
Everyone living in a polis was automatically a citizen.
Citizenship meant only military service.
Ancient citizenship and modern citizenship were identical.
questions.explanation: Ancient political communities distinguished recognized citizens from other residents with different statuses.

questions.prompt: Which comparison is most historically defensible?
choices: Persia and Athens can be ranked on a single universal scale from tyranny to freedom.
Persian imperial administration and Athenian citizen government organized power differently, and both must be analyzed for participation, exclusion, hierarchy, coercion, and context.
Athens represents every Greek polis.
Local autonomy in Persia meant subjects had equal political citizenship throughout the empire.
questions.explanation: Comparative analysis should identify real institutional differences while examining exclusions and power within each system.

shortResponse.prompt: Using at least three specific pieces of evidence and at least two source types, compare how the Achaemenid Persian Empire and Greek poleis organized political membership, diversity, military power, and participation. Explain one limitation of a simple “freedom versus tyranny” interpretation.
shortResponse.exemplar: Full-credit work makes a defensible comparison, uses accurate evidence from Persia and at least one Greek polis, incorporates at least two source types, distinguishes participation from exclusion, and explains why a binary freedom-versus-tyranny frame is incomplete.
